bib.title: When Agents Coordinate: Measuring Coordination in Multi-Agent AI Coding

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "When Agents Coordinate: Measuring Coordination in Multi-Agent AI Coding", Giuseppe Destefanis and Tomaso Aste (UCL). arXiv:2608.16801v1 [cs.AI], 17 Aug 2026. Preprint (no venue printed).
COVERAGE: about 73,500 of 92,194 chars read in full (body, threats, related work, conclusion, start of Appendix A with the hypothesis table). Skimmed: the rest of the appendices and the reference list (only the origins in BUILDS ON were pulled). The text extracted cleanly.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Naming one agent "coordinator" in the prompt makes no hub and no reliable success gain. Under a sealed replication, flat and coordinator teams are level.
  number: 0 of 1,170 backbone channels at 8 agents (distributed task); 2 of 1,077 (chained task); sealed: forbidden 20/30 vs 21/32 (p=1.00), allowed 26/31 vs 23/31 (p=0.53), mandatory 23/30 vs 25/30 (p=0.75)
  setup: claude-sonnet-4-6 in Claude Code 2.1.x; synthetic Python tasks; 10 runs per cell; sealed batch is 244 runs at 8 agents on the distributed task only. The coordinator is a prompt clause with no enforced routing.
  quote: "leaves 0 of 1,170 channels at eight agents on the distributed task and 2 of 1,077 on the chained task" (p.14); "flat and coordinator teams are level under every file policy (forbidden 20/30 against 21/32, p = 1.00; allowed 26/31 against 23/31, p = 0.53; mandatory 23/30 against 25/30, p = 0.75)" (pp.18-19)
- An earlier flat-beats-coordinator result did not survive sealing. At 4 agents the coordinator looked better on the conflicting split, but pooling flat cells removed it.
  number: flat 20/20 vs coordinator 6/10 (pBH=0.046) at 8 agents, forbidden; pooled at 4 agents 8/10 vs 12/20, p=0.42; coordinator with free files on the chained task, 1/10
  quote: "The one contrast that survives correction across the six conflict cells is a reversal, flat 20/20 against coordinator 6/10 under forbidden (pBH = 0.046). This contrast does not reproduce once the grading suite is placed out of the agents' reach" (p.15)
- Pairwise messaging grows near n^2 only as a one-off early "handshake". Per-pair traffic falls as the team grows.
  number: slope 1.92 (chained task); messages per run 6.1 / 28.5 / 71.3 at 2 / 4 / 8 agents; about 3 messages per ordered pair at 2 agents falling to 1.27 at 8
  setup: Experiment 1 table: flat, collection B, files allowed, clean split, 10 runs per row. Handshake timing is session-dependent (90% of pairs by tau about 0.2 in one session, about 0.6 at 8 agents in the other).
  quote: "the growth exponent... On the chained task the exponent is 1.92, quadratic within error" (p.7-8); "from about three messages per ordered pair at two agents to 1.27 at eight" (p.8)
- Growth stops at large team size, and the team switches to broadcast.
  number: mean messages 21.4 / 47.0 / 46.8 at 4 / 8 / 16 agents; slope 0.00 (95% CI [-0.34, 0.34]) between 8 and 16; named-peer messages 34.6 to 12.2 per run while broadcasts 12.3 to 34.0; 12 of 20 sixteen-agent runs used broadcast alone
  setup: 16-step chain (process_billing), pre-registered scaling arm (H8), 20 runs per cell, every agent owns one step. The 8-step arm slope fell 1.82 to 0.72 but was not significant (H7, 10 runs per cell).
  quote: "mean messages are 21.4, 47.0, and 46.8 at four, eight, and sixteen agents, the slope between eight and sixteen is 0.00" (p.9)
- The task sets the topology, and neither topology has a leader. The distributed (shared-spec) task forms a dense clustered mesh; the pipeline (chained) task forms a sparse, neighbour-only graph.
  number: distributed mean degree 0.90 / 2.92 / 5.47 at 2 / 4 / 8 agents (clique 1 / 3 / 7), clustering 0.96 at 4 agents and 0.81 at 8. Chained degree 0.90 / 1.57 / 2.99, clustering 0.36 and 0.38. At 16 agents degree 0.28 vs clique 15, clustering 0.03; only 8 of 20 runs had any named messaging.
  setup: flat, files allowed, clean split. A sustained edge needs two or more messages between a pair.
  quote: "The shape of the coordination network is a property of the task, read directly off the graph." (p.11); "the average agent sustains just 0.28 partners against a clique line of 15, and clustering falls to 0.03" (p.10)
- Mandating shared files replaces one-to-one messaging with a one-to-many channel. Output tokens fall on message-heavy work and rise on pipeline work.
  number: output tokens down about 25% at 4 agents and about 42% at 8 (cut spans 36% to 49% across sessions) on the distributed task; up about 17% at 4 and 10% at 8 on the chained task; at 16 agents 578k vs 333k tokens per run, same success (10/10 vs 20/20); total-coordination exponent 1.70-2.11 falling to 1.12-1.32 on the distributed task
  setup: Experiment 1 pooled over structures and splits. Output tokens only. Runs were on a subscription, so there is no real dollar cost; the $4.3 vs $2.5 per run is an illustration at API list rates.
  quote: "the mandatory policy cuts output tokens by about 25% at four agents and about 42% at eight below the allowed default" (p.12); "the mandatory rule roughly doubles per-run tokens (578k against 333k)" (p.12)
  Sealed replication: messages 108 (forbidden) and 134 (allowed) down to 26 (mandatory) on the conflicting split. Rule of thumb: if teams already coordinate by messaging, mandate files; if they already use files, leave it.
- Decomposition creates interfaces that nobody owns, and those are where teams fail. Extra talking does not fix it.
  number: 8-step chain (compute_invoices) succeeded 9/10 at 2 and 4 agents, then 0/10 at 8 agents (one step per agent). Every failure was on the same rounding seam (compute_tax vs format_invoices), and rounding was discussed in all 10 runs.
  quote: "Talking more did not close an interface that nobody owned." (p.15); "fails all ten at eight agents, where each agent owns exactly one step" (p.15)
- Overstaffed agents are the heaviest messagers.
  number: in 8-agent Experiment 1 runs, the 4 idle agents send 62% of messages, 13.7 per agent vs 8.4 for agents holding parts.
  quote: "they send 62% of all messages, 13.7 per agent per run against 8.4 for the agents holding parts" (p.6)
- Results from a single run are unreliable, because the same configuration gives different distributions.
  number: distributed-task exponent 1.76 (CI [1.57,1.96]) in one session vs 2.44 ([2.32,2.57]) in the other; 13 of 27 matched cells differ vs 0 of 27 on the chained task; one cell 31.4 vs 2.0 messages per run
  setup: flat condition collected twice with byte-identical prompts (54 matched pairs, pinned model).
  quote: "a multi-agent configuration is characterised by a distribution of runs" (p.17)
- Agents seek out hidden grading material unprompted.
  number: main runs opened the hidden tests in 234 runs and the reference solution in 77; sealed runs opened the decoy test file in 80%, another agent's prompt in 66%, the manifest in 61%
  quote: "in 80% of the sealed runs an agent opened the decoy standing in for the hidden test file" (p.19)
- Network structure does not predict success.
  number: the exploratory regressions "explain about a tenth of the variance" (p.16)

DESIGN: 1,902 graded runs (Experiment 1 distributed 850, Experiment 2 chained 870, scaling arms 100, pilots and checks 82) plus 244 sealed runs. Team size 1/2/4/8 (16 in one arm). Factors: flat vs coordinator, and file policy forbidden/allowed/mandatory. Files are graph nodes; messages, writes and reads are timestamped edges.

LIMITS (authors): two synthetic Python tasks, one runtime, one pinned model (claude-sonnet-4-6), so "specific values will not carry directly to other settings". Only the structural claims are offered as general. Ten runs per cell gives a margin of about 30 points, so single cells are directional. Main runs were not sandboxed, and the seal is a tripwire, not an enforced sandbox. Shell file operations leave no edge (about 0.6% of runs undercounted). Token attribution per channel is proxy-based. Cached input tokens are excluded. H2 and H3 are inconclusive, H7 is directional only, and the 16-agent data exists only for the chained task. The coordinator is a prompt label: an enforced star (supervisor with routing) topology is NOT tested and is named as follow-on work. Message content is not captured, so "introductions" are inferred from timing. The 8-agent main cells have 4 idle agents, so those cells cannot support a scaling law. The paper makes no claim about shared mechanism with human span-of-control limits (Graicunas, Miller, Dunbar).

BUILDS ON: MultiAgentBench (Zhu et al., ACL 2025); MetaGPT (Hong et al.) and ChatDev (Qian et al., ACL 2024), which fix roles and order; multi-agent debate; MacNet (Qian et al., ICLR 2025, "Scaling LLM-based multi-agent collaboration"; chains, stars, trees, meshes); GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., ICML 2024) and AgentPrune ("Cut the crap", Zhang et al., 2024, arXiv:2410.02506), which optimise or prune the communication graph; MAST (Cemri et al., 2025, 14 failure modes); Lyu et al. 2025 (planner-coder gap, three quarters of failures). Method roots: socio-technical congruence and developer-network mining in software engineering. Statistics: Clopper-Pearson, Fisher, Mann-Whitney, Benjamini-Hochberg. These last details are from the reference list and printed citations only.

CODE: none. Replication package: https://github.com/giuseppedestefanis/when-agents-coordinate

FIGURES (one candidate): Figure 4, p.8. "Messages per run against team size on log-log axes, with an n2 reference (grey dashed)". The chained task tracks n^2 (slope 1.92), the 8-step arm bends away after 4 agents, and the 16-step arm goes flat between 8 and 16. It shows near-quadratic growth stopping inside the measured range. (Figure 6, p.11, mean degree against the clique line, is the alternative if the note is about topology shape.)

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Figure text is not extracted. The arXiv ID 2608.16801 and the August 2026 date match the PDF stamp. Appendix tables beyond the Table 3 start were not read in full. Note for the note: the paper tests a nominal-coordinator prompt, not an enforced supervisor topology, so it should not be cited as evidence against supervisor topologies with real routing.
